_comment: Upstream end-of-security-support dates, per branch. The index carries them so the GUI can warn
on a version nobody patches any more. It does not carry them so anything can be hidden: PHP is
offered from 7.0 upwards on purpose, which is years past every date below, because the people
who reach for a local development environment rather than a container are very often the people
maintaining something old. A warning is the honest answer; refusing to install is not.
**Not one date in this file is anybody's opinion.** Every one of them is transcribed from a
machine-readable document its publisher maintains, and `tools/eol.py --check` proves it against
that document — six kinds, six publishers, no third-party mirror; the URLs are in that file's
docstring and the per-kind blocks below name the field each date was read from. When a
publisher moves a schedule, `tools/eol.py --update` transcribes it again and the diff is
committed. Do not edit a date here by hand: the check would fail on it, which is the point.
They are written down at all, rather than fetched when the index is generated, because the
index has to be rebuildable from the release assets alone years after a line was packed and
after its publisher has stopped listing it. A generator that called six APIs would produce a
different index depending on the day it ran. So the fetch happens on a schedule and its result
is committed — see `.github/workflows/check-eol.yml`, and P10 in docs/roadmap.md for why the
check cannot live in the recipes.
Each publisher's document is transcribed in full rather than trimmed to the lines this
repository offers, which is why PHP 4.3 and PostgreSQL 6.3 are here. A subset cannot be
checked — nothing distinguishes a line deliberately left out from one forgotten — and a full
table costs nothing, since mkindex.py reads the lines it needs and ignores the rest.
_node_comment: nodejs/Release's own schedule.json, field `end`. Node.js lines are keyed by major, not by
major.minor: a Node release line is 22, and 22.11 is a patch of it. That is why mkindex.py looks
a version up both ways. The odd-numbered lines are Current and last about eight months, which is
why several of them are already past.
_python_comment: peps.python.org/api/release-cycle.json, field `end_of_life` — the document the developer's
guide itself consumes to draw the chart on devguide.python.org/versions. Keyed by major.minor
because that is what a Python release line is.
Upstream states a line that has not ended yet to the month — `2030-10`, not a day — and the
rounding to the last day of that month is upstream's too: devguide's own generator resolves the
same field that way before drawing it. So 3.14 ends on 31 October 2030 because python.org says
October 2030 and python.org says October means the whole of October.
_ruby_comment: ruby/www.ruby-lang.org's _data/branches.yml — the file the branches page is generated from —
field `eol_date`, falling back to `expected_eol_date`. **Read this block before touching a Ruby
date: this is the kind P10 caught being wrong, and it was wrong in three different ways.**
3.2 was written 2026-03-31 and upstream says 2026-04-01. Off by a day, from a page whose prose
says March and whose data says 1 April.
3.4 and 4.0 carried dates nobody published. Ruby is the only one of the six kinds here that
does not state a future date: `eol_date` is filled in when a branch actually ends. Both entries
had been extrapolated from Ruby's habit of ending a line on 31 March about four years on, which
is a good guess and was still this repository's guess printed in a field that means "upstream
says". They are gone, and their lines are undated until upstream dates them.
3.3's number was right and its source was not. A branch in security maintenance carries an
`expected_eol_date`, which is transcribed — refusing it would leave 3.3 undated while PHP 8.5
carries a date four years further out, and PHP's, Node's and Python's future dates are plans
that can move too. `tools/eol.py --check` prints the field each date came from, so an
1.9.3 and 2.0.0 are named the way upstream names them, three parts, and mkindex.py's lookup
tries major.minor then major and so will never match either. Both are a decade past their end
and far below the recipe's floor; they are here because this file transcribes the document
_caddy_comment: Caddy has no entry, and the absence is deliberate rather than pending. The project publishes
no end-of-life schedule: there is one supported line, 2.x, and support means the newest patch
of it. A date invented here would be worse than none — the GUI would warn about a version that
is perfectly current, or stay silent about one that is not, and either way it would be this
file's opinion rather than upstream's. `mkindex.py` leaves a package undated when its kind is
absent, which is the honest answer.
The same is true of every service whose publisher rolls support forward instead of branching
it. Four kinds are in that position — caddy, nginx, redis and memcached — which is why
`tools/eol.py` has six sources and not ten, and it is the one thing the check cannot notice:
if Caddy ever starts publishing a schedule, nothing here will say so. Re-ask it when a kind's
packaging is next touched, the way P8 and P9 did.
_redis_memcached_comment: Asked at P8 and left undated, which is a different answer from Caddy's above: Redis does branch
— 7.2, 7.4 and every 8.x line took a patch on the same day in July 2026 — so a date is the
right shape for it. Upstream simply does not state one for Redis Open Source anywhere.
**And searching for one leads somewhere worse than nothing.** redis.io publishes a detailed
product lifecycle with dated majors, and it is for Redis Software, the commercial cluster
product, whose version numbers overlap the open-source ones without meaning the same thing —
it lists a 7.22 and a 7.8, which Redis Open Source has never had, beside a 7.2 and a 7.4,
which it has. Transcribing that table into this file would date every artifact here against
another product's support window and nothing would look wrong. P10 read this and did not reach
for the mirror; it turned out not to need endoflife.date for anything, because all six kinds
that do state a schedule state it themselves.
memcached publishes no schedule of any kind and maintains one line, so it is Caddy's case.
_nginx_comment: Caddy's case again, and asked at P9 rather than assumed from the fact that nginx has numbered
branches. It does have them — 1.26, 1.28 and 1.30 all exist — but only the newest stable line
and the newest mainline ever take a fix, so a branch is unsupported the moment the next one
appears rather than on a date anybody announced. nginx publishes no lifecycle schedule and no
end-of-life dates of any kind; its security advisories name the versions a flaw was fixed in,
which is a different fact. A date invented here would be this file's opinion, so there is none
What the index can say instead is already in each artifact: the compiled cells name the OpenSSL
they were built against and the borrowed Windows one names the OpenSSL upstream built it
against, in `smoke.openssl`. For a web server that is the number worth watching, and it is
_mariadb_comment: `tools/mariadb.py` resolves a version against. Keyed by major.minor because that is what a
MariaDB series is. This was the first entry in the file to be read from a publisher rather than
typed, and P10 made it the pattern rather than the exception; `mariadb.py` still prints the date
it saw on every run, which catches a moved schedule at pack time as well as on the schedule.
13.0 and 13.1 are listed by upstream as RC and Preview with no date, so they are not here. A
date will appear the week either one goes stable and the check next runs.
10.6 is here and is past — 6 July 2026 — for the same reason PHP 7.0 is offered: someone
maintaining an application against it is exactly the person who reaches for a local development
environment. A warning is the honest answer; refusing to install is not.
_postgres_comment: postgresql.org/versions.json, field `eolDate` — the same document `tools/postgres.py` resolves
a version against, and it states every major back to 6.3. Keyed by major alone, because that is
what a PostgreSQL release line is: 18 is the line and 18.6 is a patch of it, which is why
mkindex.py tries both spellings. `tools/postgres.py` prints the date it saw on every run.
13 has a date here and cannot be packed: EDB's macOS archive for 13 is Intel-only, so a 13
packed here would mean two different things on the two Apple cells, and the recipe's floor is
14 — the reason is written up in P7. The date is present because this file transcribes
upstream's document rather than this repository's catalogue, and the two are not the same list.
_php_comment: php.net/releases/branches.php — JSON, no query string, and the machine half of the data that
renders supported-versions.php. Keyed by major.minor because that is what a PHP branch is.
The field is `security_support_end`, not `active_support_end`, and the choice is the whole
meaning of this file: a branch in security-only support is still patched, and the date the GUI
should warn about is the day the patches stop. PHP states both, two years apart, which makes
picking the wrong one a warning that fires two years early on every branch at once.
3.0 is in upstream's document with an end of 20 October 2000 and is in this one for the reason
the top of the file gives — the document is transcribed, not curated. php.net keeps it in the
list to save a special case in its own code, which is a fine reason for it to be there and no
reason for this file to argue.
